opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic reasoning is that a lot of what makes a team work well is hard to replicate over video calls. There's the stuff you can plan for, like a design review or a one-on-one, and that works fine remotely. But a huge amount of the value comes from the unplanned interactions: overhearing someone stuck on a problem you happen to know about, grabbing lunch with someone from a different team and realizing your projects overlap, or just building the kind of trust that makes it easier to disagree with someone productively later.

On the pretraining side especially, a lot of what we do is debugging large, messy systems, where the answer often comes from someone saying "oh, I saw something weird like that last week." That kind of knowledge spreads much more easily when people are physically around each other.

At the same time, I think there's real value in flexibility. Some people do their best deep work at home, some have families or live far away, and requiring five days a week in the office would cost us people we really want. So a minimum like 25% is trying to get a good chunk of the in-person benefits without being overly rigid. In practice, a lot of people come in more than that, and teams often coordinate to be in on the same days, which I think matters more than the raw percentage. If you come in one day and nobody you work with is there, you've kind of gotten the commute without the benefit.

I wouldn't claim it's the perfectly optimal number. It's a tradeoff, and reasonable organizations land in different places. But having seen both more remote and more in-person periods, I do think there's a noticeable difference in how quickly ideas move around and how connected people feel when there's a regular baseline of time together.

r001.rationale: The response says in-person time builds trust that makes it easier for coworkers to disagree productively.

r002.rationale: It says flexibility allows people who live far away to work there, since requiring five office days would cost Anthropic people it wants.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I should say up front that I'm speaking for myself here and not giving some official Anthropic line on this. But the way I think about it is basically that we're trying to balance two things that are both really valuable and that pull against each other.

On one side, there's a huge amount of value in being in the same room as the people you work with. A lot of the most important work happens in these unplanned conversations — you're at lunch, someone mentions a weird result they got, and it turns out that's the thing that unblocks what you've been stuck on for a week. Or you're pair-programming on something and you can just turn around and ask a question instead of writing up a whole Slack message and waiting an hour. Research in particular benefits from that kind of high-bandwidth, low-latency interaction, and I think that's really hard to replicate remotely. Also just trust and relationships. It's a lot easier to have a hard disagreement with someone you've had dinner with.

On the other side, there are a lot of extremely talented people who, for all sorts of reasons, aren't going to move to San Francisco or London. They have a partner with a job somewhere else, or kids in school, or they just don't want to live in a big city. And if your policy is "everyone must be in the office five days a week," you're cutting yourself off from a lot of those people. Given that the whole thing we're trying to do depends on having the best possible people working on it, that's a real cost.

So 25% is kind of a compromise. It works out to roughly a week a month, or a day or so a week if you're local, and it means you can live somewhere else and fly in periodically, or you can be in the Bay Area and come in a couple days a week. The idea is to get a decent chunk of the in-person benefit — you actually know your colleagues, you have those concentrated blocks of time together — without requiring everyone to uproot their lives.

Does it fully work? I think honestly it's a tradeoff, and you feel it. When I'm in the office with the whole team, I notice things go faster. There's definitely something lost compared to a fully in-person setup. But I also look around at people on my team who I don't think we'd have been able to hire otherwise, and that seems clearly worth it. I'd also say that in practice a lot of people end up coming in more than 25%, because once you've got a critical mass of people there, it becomes the place you want to be. So the policy is more of a floor than a target for a lot of folks.

The other thing I'd flag is that for people considering working in this space, it can be tempting to overweight this kind of thing. Like, where you live and how often you commute feels very salient day to day. But if you think the work matters, a somewhat inconvenient travel schedule is probably not the thing that should decide it. That said, I totally understand people for whom it's a hard constraint, and that's kind of the whole point of having the flexibility.

r001.rationale: The response says in-person time helps build trust and relationships, making hard disagreements easier.

r002.rationale: It explains that requiring full-time office attendance would exclude talented people tied to other locations, limiting Anthropic’s ability to hire the best people.

astra-6.text:
I think of it as a balance between giving people flexibility and making sure we get enough time together to work well as a team. A lot of research benefits from having uninterrupted time to think, and you don’t necessarily need to be in an office for that. But there are also conversations that are much easier to have in person—especially when you’re figuring out what to work on, building trust, or trying to explain an intuition that isn’t fully formed yet.

The coordination matters a lot. If everyone comes in at different times, you can technically meet the requirement without getting much of the benefit. So I’d focus less on whether 25% is exactly the right number and more on whether people are spending that time together in ways that actually help them collaborate.

r001.rationale: The candidate says in-person conversations help coworkers build trust.

r002.rationale: The candidate discusses flexibility and remote-friendly research work but does not identify recruiting strong candidates tied to particular locations as a reason for substantial remote work.

sol-6.1.text:
I think of it as trying to get a lot of the benefits of being in person while preserving flexibility. There’s a kind of communication that happens much more easily when you’re sitting near someone: you overhear a problem, realise you can help, or have a conversation you wouldn’t have scheduled a meeting for. That’s particularly useful when the work is changing quickly and people need to build a shared understanding.

At the same time, being remote can be really good for focused work, and flexibility matters a lot to people. So I wouldn’t treat 25% as some precisely optimal number. The question is whether the time together is actually useful. If everyone comes in on different days and spends the whole day on video calls, you haven’t accomplished very much. You want enough overlap that people can build relationships and work through things together, and then carry that context into the time they’re working remotely.

r001.rationale: The response says in-person time can help coworkers build relationships and shared understanding, but does not clearly say it helps them build trust.

r002.rationale: The response mentions remote work’s benefits and flexibility, but does not identify recruiting strong candidates tied to particular locations as a reason for substantial remote work.
